blocks.html: Lesson 4 of 4. This lesson shows what a client experiences in an OASYS engagement. We offer a do-it-yourself option, but OneAccord always recommends the full coached engagement, because that's where clients get the most value. The lesson ends with a short exercise: explaining OASYS to a prospect.

blocks.html:
Three ways owners approach it

  1. Do it yourself, alone: thousands of owners read Traction or Scaling Up and start implementing on their own.
  2. Do it yourself with group coaching: some support, shared with other companies.
  3. Done for you with an implementer coach (OASYS): we help set up the tools, facilitate the initial and ongoing planning sessions, and coach the leadership team.

Like a coach on the sidelines, we're not better at the game than the players. We're better at watching, knowing what to look for, and helping them improve.

For prospects who can't afford a full engagement yet, we can set them up on ninety.io to self-implement and stay their go-to resource when bigger issues come up. Lead with the full engagement.

blocks.html:
How success is measured

Success isn't one end goal like selling the company. It's getting steadily better at ten things that serve the three owner objectives:

  1. A solid strategy
  2. A shared vision
  3. The right people in the right seats
  4. Great teamwork
  5. The right numbers (KPIs)
  6. Consistent execution
  7. A leadership team that solves its own issues
  8. The right things getting done each 90 days
  9. Financial performance
  10. Enterprise value

The engagement journey

  1. Baseline: a OneAccord business assessment, an enterprise value appraisal, and behavioral and team assessments (for example DISC, Working Genius, and Five Dysfunctions trust-building).
  2. Situation analysis and proposal, then agreement with the owner or CEO.
  3. Implementation workshops: Foundations, Goals and Vision. These can be full days or several half days, virtual or in person.
  4. Weekly meetings: we coach the leadership team's first weekly meetings, then the agenda rolls out through the company.
  5. Quarterly planning: dates set for a rolling 12 months; we facilitate each 90-day session, ideally in person.
  6. Annual retreat: about a year in, a two-day off-site for long-term vision and the next 90-day plan.
  7. Graduation: when the client can sustain the cadence on their own.

blocks.promptHtml:
Final exercise: explain OASYS in about a minute.

A CPA you work with introduces you to one of her clients, the owner of a growing manufacturing company: "He's stretched thin, his team isn't aligned, and he says he'd like to sell in five or six years. I told him you might be able to help."

Write what you'd say to the owner, in about 150 to 250 words, the way you'd actually say it.
rubric: Connects to his situation and at least one owner objective (time freedom, alignment on goals, or enterprise value and exit readiness)
Explains what OASYS does: a strategic plan plus an upgraded operating system, run on ninety.io, so the plan actually gets executed
Describes how an engagement works at a high level (assessment, implementation workshops, 90-day planning cadence, annual retreat, coaching until they graduate)
Explains why the coached approach beats doing it alone, without dismissing the DIY option
Proposes a clear, low-pressure next step and does not quote prices
blocks.coachContext: OneAccord's OASYS Strategic Planning practice (older materials and videos call it SPE, Strategic Planning and Execution; Doug sometimes says 'Oasis') helps clients build a strategic plan AND upgrade their Business Operating System (BOS) so the plan actually gets executed. OASYS is OneAccord's branded BOS, built on the Ninety OS model and run on the ninety.io software platform. Doug Hall presents the training videos and helped launch the practice; he has coached business operating systems since 2016 (first EOS-certified implementer in Washington State in 2017, later Pinnacle Business Guides and Scaling Up), and takes an independent, best-of-breed approach. The practice currently has no dedicated lead; Nick Anderson is the contact for questions about it. Three owner objectives: (1) achieve the business purpose and goals (mission, vision, values, legacy, aligned team); (2) increase the owner's time freedom by building a self-managing company with a strong leadership team; (3) optimize enterprise value, mainly by reducing owner dependence and improving financial performance, which opens exit options including a financial exit or an operating exit (e.g. CEO emeritus). If an owner is comfortable on all three, they won't buy; there must be pain in at least one, or a vague dissatisfaction, a desire to be a 'category of one', or a sense the owner can't take the company to the next level alone (humility and hunger). Common strategic planning failures: no clear direction, misaligned teams, poor follow-through, 'shelfware' plans that never get executed (the execution gap), firefighting, bias, complexity. Strategic planning answers: where are we now, where do we want to be, how do we get there. Building blocks: vision, mission, core values, SWOT, long-term objectives, 90-day priorities ('Rocks'), KPIs, action plans, accountability structure. The practice is horizontal (no industry expertise needed), hired by the CEO, and works with the leadership team (the CEO's strategic direct reports). Engagement: onboarding and initial implementation, then a strategic plan refresh every 90 days anchored by an annual 2-day off-site retreat, typically as an annual plan of work billed as a monthly retainer. Do not quote prices; a managing principal guides pricing. It is a top-down upgrade that can cross-sell into functional work (marketing, sales, operations, interim/fractional leaders) and vice versa; OneAccord refers out legal and some CFO work. Every company that makes payroll already has a BOS: its current way of leading and managing (often informal, like a fish not knowing it's in water), shaped by the founder, shiny objects the CEO brings back from peer groups, and new managers' habits. Typical informal BOS tools: occasional off-site planning, a maybe-written strategic plan, a budget, monthly financials, weekly staff meetings, one-on-ones, all-hands, annual performance reviews. Upgrading means getting uncomfortable before getting comfortable again, so change management matters. Costs of an informal BOS: chaos, wasted time, inconsistent results, stalled growth, over-reliance on individuals, reduced company value. Deming: every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets. Owners can upgrade functions (marketing, sales, ops, finance) or upgrade the BOS and leadership team; prospects for OASYS usually find the leadership team has become the limiting factor. BOS lineage: Gerber (E-Myth), Jack Stack (Great Game of Business), Andy Grove and John Doerr (OKRs), Verne Harnish (Rockefeller Habits, Scaling Up), Gino Wickman (EOS/Traction), Franklin Covey (4 Disciplines of Execution), plus Lencioni and Collins; Ninety OS is the first software-based BOS and covers the best of EOS, 4DX, OKRs and parts of Scaling Up. Foundational tools: one-page strategic plan (core values, purpose, 10-year, 3-year, 1-year goals, 90-day Rocks), org chart with functional accountability, KPI scorecards with lead and lag measures, weekly team meetings with a set agenda, quarterly planning cadence. Ninety OS has 9 core competencies (vision, customer, goals, people, structure, data, meetings, process, enterprise value), continuously improved by working the system. ninety.io holds vision and planning, scorecard, Rocks, issues, meeting rhythms, people tools, processes, to-dos. Client options: do-it-yourself alone (read Traction), DIY with group coaching, or done-for-you implementer coaching (OneAccord's recommended full engagement). The coach is like a sports coach on the sidelines: not better at the game, better at watching and coaching. OneAccord always recommends the full coached engagement but can help budget-limited clients self-implement on ninety.io and stay their go-to resource. Success = steady improvement on ten factors (solid strategy, shared vision, right people in right seats, teamwork, right numbers/KPIs, consistent execution, solving issues / self-managing team, getting the right stuff done in 90-day focus, financial performance, enterprise value), not a single end goal. Process: baseline benchmarks (OneAccord business assessment, enterprise value appraisal, behavioral assessments such as DISC or Predictive Index, team tools such as Working Genius and Five Dysfunctions trust-building) -> situation analysis and proposal -> agreement with owner/CEO -> implementation workshops (foundations, goals, vision; full days or several half days, virtual or in person) -> coach the weekly team meetings and roll the agenda down -> schedule quarterly planning dates for a rolling 12 months -> facilitate 90-day off-sites (ideally in person) -> first annual 2-day retreat about a year in -> 'graduate' the client when they can sustain the cadence themselves. This is the capstone exercise of the overview course. Grade generously on wording but strictly on substance: the learner should sound like a credible, consultative OneAccord principal.
